value_chain_position: Peruvian precious/base-metals producer; consolidated revenue is mostly silver/gold, with copper exposure carried as an equity-method affiliate (Cerro Verde), not consolidated sales.
cost_curve_verified: Disagree, and the proxy is the one that is wrong: the screener places Buenaventura in the highest-cost quartile of its eight-name peer group (12th percentile), yet the company's own first-half 2026 direct-operations margin was 57.5% ($663.4M of profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation on $1,153.6M of revenue), against 55.7% for Pan American Silver and 53.7% for Hecla Mining on a trailing basis — that is at or above the median of its named competitors. The company publishes no consolidated all-in sustaining cost per ounce (only an all-in cost 'expressed in terms of copper' plus a per-unit cost-applicable-to-sales table), which is a real disclosure gap, so the margin comparison is the best available cross-check.
gm_trajectory: Expanding year-on-year, flattening sequentially. Gross margin went from 44.7% in the second quarter of 2025 ($165.2M on $369.5M) to 58.6% in the second quarter of 2026 ($310.2M on $529.0M) while revenue rose 43%. But revenue fell 15% sequentially, from $622.5M in the first quarter of 2026 to $529.0M in the second, on broadly stable volumes — the silver price is already arriving in the top line even though margin has not yet given ground.
bull_thesis:
Buenaventura is a genuinely profitable Peruvian miner whose most valuable asset is largely invisible in its own income statement, and the market appears to be paying very little for the rest of the company once that asset is properly credited.

Start with the piece you can price from an arm's-length transaction. Buenaventura owns 19.58% of Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde, one of the world's larger long-life copper mines, operated by Freeport-McMoRan. In the second quarter of 2026 Freeport bought 2.0 million Cerro Verde shares in the open market for $107 million — $53.50 a share, which values all 350.06 million shares at $18.7 billion and Buenaventura's stake at roughly $3.7 billion. The Lima listing currently marks the whole company higher still, at about PEN 80.9 billion (roughly $22.8 billion), implying $4.5 billion for the stake. Buenaventura's entire market value is $8.13 billion at $32.00 a share. So somewhere between 45% and 55% of the market capitalisation is a minority interest in a top-tier copper mine that has already paid Buenaventura $274.1 million of cash dividends in 2026 alone, including $117.5 million received on 24 July — after quarter-end, so not yet in the reported $758.9 million cash balance.

Strip the stake out at a conservative $3.1 billion (a 15% discount to the Freeport mark for being a non-controlling holding) and the market is paying about $4.9 billion of enterprise value for everything else. Everything else generated $663.4 million of profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the first half of 2026 alone. Even repricing that at today's much lower metal prices — roughly $0.95–1.05 billion a year — the residual business is on about 5 times profit, against Pan American Silver at 8.3 times and Hecla Mining at 12.0 times on the same trailing measure. That is the discount.

The operating story underneath is better than the headlines suggest. Yumpag, the silver flagship, produced 2.32 million ounces in the second quarter — about two-thirds of consolidated silver output — and just received approval to lift throughput from 1,000 to 1,200 tonnes a day. Operations vice-president Juan Carlos Ortiz said on the 2026-07-31 call that the combination of that throughput gain and a switch from diesel generators to national-grid power should cut Yumpag's operating cost 'in the level of 15%-17% lower than the operating cost of the first half of the year' by year-end. Separately, the price-based escalator in the silver concentrate contracts — which inflated first-half unit costs — resets from a $35 per ounce base to a $50 base from September (commercial vice-president Aldo Massa, 2026-07-31). Both are dated, specific and mechanical rather than aspirational.

The balance sheet is clean and independently verified: $758.9 million of cash against $692 million of total debt at 30 June 2026, a net cash position of about $67 million, and the 2026 bond redeemed at par in July 2025. Net debt to profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation is negative. Permitting — the thing that usually kills Peruvian mining plans — has gone well: the Coimolache operating permit in September 2025, the San Gabriel operating permit and water licence in 2026, El Brocal to 17,000 tonnes a day, and an approved environmental impact assessment at the Trapiche copper project.

San Gabriel, for all its troubles, adds reserve life the company badly needed: 15.3 million tonnes of proven and probable reserves at 3.71 grams of gold per tonne — about 1.8 million ounces — with a potential 16-year life and a target above 100,000 ounces a year once stable. Management now guides steady state to the middle of 2027. At today's $4,157.60 gold, 100,000 ounces at a plausible all-in cost around $1,500 is roughly $260 million a year of profit that does not exist in any trailing number.

Finally, two optional pieces sit on top. The strategic review of Orcopampa, Tambomayo and Julcani is live, and selling late-life mines into a high gold price would convert depleting assets into cash. And Antofagasta plc has held an approximately 19% equity interest since December 2023 — a strategic industry shareholder on the register, never once discussed on any of these five calls.

What has to hold for this to work: silver needs to stabilise somewhere near $60 rather than continuing down; San Gabriel needs to hit stable throughput by mid-2027 without a fourth guidance cut; Cerro Verde needs to keep distributing; and Peru's incoming government needs to leave the tax and royalty regime alone.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not need the company to fail. It only needs the metal price to keep doing what it has already started doing, because Buenaventura's reported earnings power is a photograph taken at the top of the silver market and the company has explicitly chosen to carry that risk naked.

Here is the number that matters. Buenaventura's first half of 2026 was earned at an average realised silver price of $94.53 an ounce and an average realised gold price of $4,599 (company production release, 2026-07-16; second-quarter realisations were $89.52 and $4,342). Today silver trades at $60.18 and gold at $4,157.60. Silver is roughly half of Buenaventura's gross metal value, gold about a fifth, copper about a quarter. Weighting today's prices against the first-half basket gives a decline of about 19%. Annualise the first half — $2.31 billion of revenue and $1.33 billion of profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation from direct operations — and reprice it, and you get roughly $1.87 billion of revenue and $0.95–1.05 billion of profit. That is not a disaster. It is simply the top of management's own February 2026 guidance of $800 million to $1.0 billion, which the market appears to have forgotten it ever gave. The trailing $1.22 billion (company definition) or $1.52 billion (screener definition) is not a run rate, and any multiple computed on it is a mirage. The sequential revenue drop already visible — $622.5 million in the first quarter to $529.0 million in the second, on stable volumes — is the leading edge of exactly this.

The torque runs both ways and it is bigger than the screener says. The deterministic proxy claims a 10% metal move swings profit by 9.5%. At a 55–58% margin with two-thirds of revenue commodity-linked, the true figure is 12–18%. The proxy understates the operating leverage by a third to a half — in both directions. And there is no hedge. The chief financial officer confirmed the policy on 2026-04-30: 'we prefer not to hedge for the time being.' A 25% fall in silver from here, with gold at $3,600 and copper at $5.50 a pound, takes direct-operations profit to roughly $0.62 billion — a 35% cut from today's repriced level and a 53% cut from the annualised first half.

The growth project has already failed its first test three times. San Gabriel's 2026 gold guidance went from 70,000–90,000 ounces (2025-10-31) to roughly 48,000–55,000 (2026-02-27) to 25,000–30,000 (2026-07-16). That last cut came when the plant was already built and running. The stated causes are tailings filtration and lower-than-expected metallurgical recovery — process problems, not schedule problems, and process problems are the expensive kind. Management now needs another $20–25 million (tailings filtration reinforcement plus a possible flotation circuit) and has pushed steady state to the middle of 2027. First-half output was 4,460 ounces against a mine designed for more than 100,000 a year. Anyone underwriting a San Gabriel contribution before 2028 is underwriting a management team that has been wrong about this asset three times running.

Capital discipline is drifting in the classic sector pattern. Capital spending for 2026 was guided at $385–415 million in February and is now around $500 million, plus $12 million for El Niño preparation. Carlos De Alba of Morgan Stanley pressed on exactly this in February and was answered with rain. Meanwhile the board doubled the dividend payout from 20% to 40% of prior-year net income in February 2026 — at $4,500 gold and near-$100 silver — with the chief executive tying it explicitly to 'as the prices are going well.' Raising distributions at the cycle top is the sin this sector commits every single cycle.

The crown-jewel argument cuts both ways too. Cerro Verde is a 19.58% non-controlling stake in a company Buenaventura does not run. Freeport-McMoRan raised its own holding to 55.66% in the second quarter of 2026 — control is consolidating away from the minority, not toward it. Buenaventura cannot force a distribution, cannot sell the stake without Freeport's cooperation, and cannot mark it. Cerro Verde's own reported first-half 2026 net income was $501.5 million, so Buenaventura's economic share of earnings is roughly $98 million for the half — far less than the $274.1 million of dividends it collected, which means the recent distributions are drawing down accumulated cash and are not a repeatable run rate. Any honest sum-of-the-parts applies a 15–30% minority discount, and in a copper downturn the stake's value falls with it.

The legacy asset base is thinning. Orcopampa, Tambomayo and Julcani are late-life and have been formally under review for sale since the 2025 investor day. That process has been 'close to a final decision' since February 2026 and was still undecided on 2026-07-31, with management explicitly reconsidering because prices rose — precisely backwards for a seller of depleting assets. Trapiche, the copper development option, was pushed out on the same call: 'we are gonna be spending the next year, year and a half in understanding if it is a business.'

And all of it sits in one country. Peru's presidential run-off was unresolved as of the April 2026 call; management's own comfort extended only to 'there should be some voices' asking for higher taxes and royalties. A single adverse tax, royalty or community outcome hits every asset at once. There is no diversification anywhere in this structure.

What would confirm the bear case: a fourth San Gabriel guidance cut or a slip of steady state past mid-2027; silver holding below $55; the asset-sale process being abandoned outright; or 2026 capital spending printing above $520 million.
sop_bull:
Favourable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately), assuming silver recovers to $75–80 an ounce, gold holds near $4,500, copper stays near current levels, San Gabriel reaches nameplate on the mid-2027 schedule, and the legacy-mine sales are crystallised. 254.0 million shares.

- Cerro Verde 19.58% stake, marked to the current Lima quote (about $22.8 billion for the whole company) less a 10% minority discount: $4.01 billion, or $15.80 a share.
- Direct precious and base-metals operations excluding San Gabriel, at about $1.10 billion of annual profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation and 5.75 times — still a discount to Pan American Silver's 8.3 times: $6.33 billion, or $24.90 a share.
- San Gabriel at nameplate, above 100,000 gold ounces a year from mid-2027, discounted for two years of ramp risk: $1.27 billion, or $5.00 a share.
- Coimolache (43.65% of Tantahuatay) plus the Trapiche copper option with its approved environmental permit: $0.53 billion, or $2.10 a share.
- Net cash of $67 million at 30 June 2026 plus the $117.5 million Cerro Verde dividend received 24 July: $0.18 billion, or $0.72 a share.

Total: about $12.3 billion, or $48.50 a share — roughly 52% above the $32.00 quote and about 21% above the highest published street target of $40.00 (Tanya Jakusconek, 2026-07-14).
sop_bear:
Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the precious-metals and copper cycle turns against Buenaventura: silver falls a further 25% to about $45 an ounce, gold to $3,600, copper to $5.50 a pound. The company is unhedged by stated policy, so the full move lands in earnings. 254.0 million shares.

- Direct operations: revenue falls about 19.5% from today's already-repriced $1.87 billion to roughly $1.51 billion; with only partial cost relief from the escalator reset and the Yumpag power switch, profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation falls to about $0.62 billion. At a 5.0 times trough multiple: $3.10 billion, or $12.20 a share.
- Cerro Verde 19.58% stake: Cerro Verde's own profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation falls from about $2.8 billion to roughly $2.0 billion; at 6.5 times, less its debt, the equity is about $12.6 billion; the stake is $2.47 billion, less a 20% minority discount: $1.97 billion, or $7.76 a share.
- San Gabriel at $3,600 gold, steady state slipping to 2028: $0.60 billion, or $2.36 a share.
- Coimolache plus Trapiche, with the copper option written down close to nothing: $0.25 billion, or $0.98 a share.
- Net cash eroded by roughly $500 million of 2026 capital spending against weaker cash generation: $0.15 billion, or $0.59 a share.

Total: about $6.0 billion, or $23.90 a share — roughly 26% below the $32.00 quote.

A deeper tail exists and should be stated. If silver returns to $38 and gold to $3,200 with copper at $4.50 a pound — a full bust rather than a correction — direct-operations profit falls to roughly $0.39 billion and the parts sum to about $15 a share, below the $17.34 low of the past twelve months. That is the honest reading of the two-way price sensitivity for an unhedged producer whose shares move about 1.2 times gold.
sop_fair_value: $37.00 per American Depositary Share (base case), against a live quote of $32.00 on 2026-08-04 — about 16% of upside.
sop_breakdown:
Base case, built asset by asset rather than from the reported segment table. A note on that table: the screener's segment block shows 'Corporates' at 52% of 2025 revenue, which is a legal-entity bucket (the parent company, carrying most gold and silver), not a product line. A naive segment sum-of-the-parts on those labels would be meaningless, so the parts below are the actual assets. Share count 254.0 million.

1. Cerro Verde 19.58% stake — $3.12 billion, or $12.28 a share (33% of the total). Anchored on Freeport-McMoRan's second-quarter 2026 open-market purchase of 2.0 million Cerro Verde shares for $107 million ($53.50 a share, implying $18.7 billion for the whole company and $3.67 billion for Buenaventura's holding), less a 15% discount for a non-controlling position in a company Buenaventura does not operate. This is a verified arm's-length transaction by a strategic buyer, not a modelled value.

2. Direct precious and base-metals operations excluding San Gabriel — $4.95 billion, or $19.49 a share (53%). That multiple is a deliberate discount to Pan American Silver's 8.3 times and Hecla Mining's 12.0 times, for single-country Peru risk, the absence of a consolidated all-in sustaining cost disclosure, and the late-life legacy mines.

3. 4. Coimolache (43.65%) plus Trapiche — $0.35 billion, or $1.38 a share (4%).

Sum: about $9.45 billion, or $37.22 a share, rounded to $37.00. Cross-check: the market's $8.13 billion capitalisation, less the conservatively marked Cerro Verde stake and cash, leaves about $4.9 billion for a business earning roughly $1.0 billion at today's metal prices — about 5 times. The discount is real; it is not enormous.
risk_reward: Poor at $32.00. Downside to the adverse case is $8.50 a share (to $23.50, about 27% below the quote); upside to base-case fair value is $5.00 a share (to $37.00, about 16% above). Upside to the favourable case is $16.50 (to $48.50). So the near-term skew is roughly 0.6 units of base-case reward for every unit of adverse-case risk, and only about 1.9-to-1 even against the full bull case — and the bull case requires the silver price to reverse a decline that is already under way. The asymmetry improves materially below about $27, where the Cerro Verde stake plus net cash plus the direct business at a 4.5 times trough multiple already covers the share price and San Gabriel, Trapiche and Coimolache come free.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing corporate event here is the strategic review and potential sale of three late-life mines — Orcopampa, Tambomayo and Julcani — first disclosed at the 2025 investor day. It has been serially extended and remains non-binding: on 2026-02-27 the chief executive said 'we are in the last part of making a decision' while commercial vice-president Aldo Massa simultaneously said 'we have not taken a decision yet on whether we are going to sell or not'; on 2026-07-31 the chief executive was still saying 'in this quarter, we expect to have some news of if we have arrived a final decision to sell Julcani.' No buyer, no price, no signed agreement, no contractual deadline. The other candidate event has already happened: the first San Gabriel gold pour in December 2025 and the start of commercial sales in the second quarter of 2026 are done, and the re-rate they were supposed to produce arrived as three successive guidance cuts instead. Per this lane's rules the status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict either way — Buenaventura is judged on its operating position and its discount to the parts.
consensus_delta:
The street is looking the wrong way in two directions at once, which is why the verdict is to wait rather than to buy or to pass.

First, coverage is genuinely thin and stale in structure. Only two price targets printed in the last quarter — a consensus of $37.25 with a high of $40.00 (Tanya Jakusconek, 2026-07-14, when the shares were $30.81) and a low of $34.50 (Morgan Stanley, 2026-07-08, when the shares were $28.91). That is not a street-wide view; it is two analysts. Note also that Morgan Stanley cut from $45.00 on 2026-04-08 to $34.50 three months later, a 23% reduction, which tells you the sell side is already marking down rather than defending.

Second, and more important: the published targets straddle a spot silver price that no longer exists in anyone's model. Buenaventura earned its first half at $94.53 an ounce of realised silver. Silver is $60.18 today. Any target set in April, or even in early July, was anchored on a materially higher price deck. Where we disagree with the market on the bearish side is simple — the trailing multiple that makes Buenaventura look cheap (5.3 times enterprise value to profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, 7.2 times earnings, an 8.1% free-cash-flow yield) is computed on a peak-price earnings base. Reprice it at today's metals and enterprise value to profit rises to roughly 8 times on a consolidated basis — squarely in line with Pan American Silver, not below it. The cheapness the screener sees is substantially a peak-earnings artifact.

Where we disagree on the bullish side, and it is the more interesting disagreement: nobody appears to be marking the Cerro Verde stake to the price a strategic buyer actually paid. Freeport-McMoRan bought 2.0 million Cerro Verde shares in the open market during the second quarter of 2026 for $107 million — $53.50 a share, $18.7 billion for the company, $3.67 billion for Buenaventura's 19.58%. That single line item is 45% of Buenaventura's entire market capitalisation, and it is carried on the balance sheet at historic equity-method cost, invisible to any screen. Once you credit it even conservatively at $3.12 billion, the market is paying about 5 times repriced profit for a business earning roughly $1.0 billion a year. That is a real discount. It is just not a large enough one, at $32.00, to pay for an unhedged silver book and a growth project that has missed three times.

The third street assumption worth naming as wrong: the general framing of San Gabriel as a 2026 contributor. It is not. First-half output was 4,460 ounces against guidance now cut to 25,000–30,000, and steady state is mid-2027. Anyone modelling a 2026 San Gabriel earnings contribution is modelling a rounding error.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next two to three quarters, and the pressure is arithmetic rather than existential — this company is in net cash and is not going to run out of money.

The first hit is the second-half revenue reset. The second quarter of 2026 already showed it: revenue fell 15% sequentially from $622.5 million to $529.0 million on stable volumes. Third-quarter realisations will be struck against a silver price that has fallen from a $89.52 second-quarter realisation to $60.18 spot. Expect a third-quarter revenue print materially below the second quarter's and a profit line closer to $200 million than to $277 million from direct operations. The market has not yet seen Buenaventura report a genuinely down quarter in this cycle, and the first one usually reprices the multiple more than the earnings.

The second hit is capital spending. Full-year 2026 capital spending is now guided at roughly $500 million against $385–415 million said in February, of which $200–220 million went out in the first half — meaning the back half is the heavier half, at the same time the revenue line is falling. Add $12 million of El Niño preparation and $20–25 million of San Gabriel tailings and flotation fixes. Free cash flow in the second half will compress hard from the trailing $656 million pace, and the buffer is the Cerro Verde dividend, not operations.

The third is the seasonal and weather risk itself. Management authorised the extra $12 million specifically because of an early warning of a strong El Niño, with heavy rain expected from December 2026. The rainy season is exactly what derailed the San Gabriel earthworks a year ago — the projects vice-president's February 2026 explanation for the capital overrun was literally that 'we are currently in the middle of the rainy season. So you keep finding things.' The same window is about to open again on a plant whose tailings facility is the constraint.

The fourth is a fourth San Gabriel guidance cut. Filtered-tailings compaction was only due to begin in the third quarter of 2026 and undercut mining below cemented fill was still ahead as of the July call. Both are the things that have gone wrong. A further cut, or a slip of steady state past mid-2027, is a live possibility on the October 2026 call.

The fifth is Peru. The presidential run-off was unresolved as of the April 2026 call, and while management is sanguine about the incoming congress, a single adverse tax, royalty or community outcome hits every asset simultaneously.

What is not a risk: solvency. Net cash of $67 million at 30 June, $758.9 million of gross cash, no near-term maturity wall after the 2026 notes were redeemed at par in July 2025, a current ratio of 2.59, and a further $117.5 million of Cerro Verde dividends banked on 24 July. There is no cash-burn hump and no refinancing cliff. The valley here is one of earnings and sentiment, not survival.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical, forced-selling event here, and it would be wrong to promise one.

The shareholder base is not yield-dependent. Buenaventura's dividend is a percentage-of-earnings policy — lifted to 40% of prior-year net income in February 2026 — not a fixed payout. It self-adjusts downward with earnings, which means a lower dividend next year is arithmetic rather than a cut, and income funds do not own this stock for a variable emerging-market miner's payout that yields roughly 3%. There is no yield cohort to flush.

What exists instead is a slower, more ordinary form of selling pressure. This is an American Depositary Share of a single-country Peruvian producer with about $11.9 million of average daily dollar volume — thin enough that a generalist or an exchange-traded-fund flow reversal moves it several percent in a day, as it did repeatedly through mid-2026 (down 4.7% on 1 June, 4.3% on 23 June, 4.2% on 28 July, and up 5.0% today). The register turns on the gold and silver complex, not on Buenaventura's operations. If the precious-metals trade unwinds, passive and momentum money leaves regardless of the sum-of-the-parts.

One genuinely notable feature of the register: Antofagasta plc has held an approximately 19% equity interest since December 2023 and has never been mentioned on any of these five earnings calls. That is a large, patient, strategic block that both suppresses free float and creates optionality — a strategic industry holder at a fifth of the company is the kind of position that either grows or eventually leaves, and neither outcome is neutral. It is not a washout risk; it is a structural feature that a buyer should be aware of.

The insider record is worth stating plainly because it is easy to misread from a screen. Across roughly the last hundred filings there have been zero open-market purchases and zero open-market sales — every filing is a grant, option or gift. Any 'insider buy ratio' on a screen for this name is noise. Management did not buy when the shares traded at $17.34 within the past year. That is not a sell signal, but it removes an argument the bull case might otherwise lean on.
forcing_function:
There is no single hard date that forces a re-rating, and this lane does not require one. What exists is a sequence of dated operating checkpoints, each of which either validates or breaks the thesis.

The nearest and most important is the third-quarter 2026 result, due late October 2026 on this company's consistent pattern of reporting in the last days of the month following quarter-end. Three things get settled there: whether San Gabriel's filtered-tailings compaction actually began in the third quarter as promised on 2026-07-31 and whether the 25,000–30,000 ounce guidance survives a fourth review; whether Yumpag's cost really fell 15–17% from first-half levels as operations vice-president Juan Carlos Ortiz committed to; and how much of the silver price decline lands in the reported margin now that the concentrate escalator base resets from $35 to $50 an ounce in September.

The second is the legacy-mine sale decision. Management has said on both the February and July 2026 calls that a decision on Orcopampa, Tambomayo and Julcani is imminent, most recently 'in this quarter' for Julcani specifically. A signed transaction at a good gold price would be genuinely clarifying: it would convert depleting assets into cash, simplify the story, and put a third-party price on assets the market currently values at nothing in particular. Continued delay is itself a mild negative.

The third is the mid-2027 San Gabriel steady state, the date management has now committed to twice. That is the point at which more than 100,000 ounces a year of gold either exists or does not.

The fourth, and the one that would most change the sum-of-the-parts, is any further Freeport-McMoRan buying of Cerro Verde stock. Freeport lifted its holding from 55.08% to 55.66% in the second quarter of 2026 at $53.50 a share. A larger purchase, or any move toward taking out the minorities, would put a hard transaction value on 45% of Buenaventura's market capitalisation — the single cleanest way for this discount to close.

None of these is a binding contractual event with a fixed payout. Buyers should size accordingly.
moderator_conclusion:
Wait for the wash-out. Buenaventura is a real business at a real discount, but not at a large enough discount to pay for what you are being asked to carry at $32.00 a share.

The honest read on the operating position, which is what this lane judges, is mixed in a specific and useful way. On cost-curve position, the deterministic proxy is simply wrong and should be discarded: it places Buenaventura in the highest-cost quartile of its peer group, but the company's own first-half 2026 direct-operations margin of 57.5% sits at or above Pan American Silver (55.7%) and Hecla Mining (53.7%). Buenaventura is a mid-cost polymetallic producer with substantial by-product credits, not a high-cost one. The genuine weakness is disclosure — it publishes no consolidated all-in sustaining cost per ounce, only an odd all-in figure 'expressed in terms of copper' and a per-unit cost-applicable-to-sales table, which makes cross-company comparison harder than it should be for a company of this size.

On contracting and reserve life, the picture is honest but short in places. Buenaventura is deliberately unhedged — the chief financial officer restated the policy on 2026-04-30 — so it is fully exposed to spot in both directions. Its concentrate sales carry named commercial mechanics rather than named offtake counterparties: price-based escalators with a $35 per ounce base through August 2026, resetting to $50 from September, and payability that drops to 60–70% on silver concentrate below 2,500 grams per tonne. There is one genuine contract, disclosed on 2026-07-31: 40,000 tonnes a year of Cerro Verde copper concentrate purchased from Freeport for resale, worth roughly $100 million of revenue at low margin. Reserve life is barbelled: Yumpag and Uchucchacua are the durable silver engine, San Gabriel adds 1.8 million ounces of proven and probable gold and a potential 16-year life, while Orcopampa, Tambomayo and Julcani are late-life and formally up for sale.

On capital discipline — the sector's besetting sin — the evidence is genuinely mixed and I will not pretend otherwise. The good: the 2026 bond was redeemed at par in July 2025, the balance sheet moved to net cash for the first time in years, and there has been no buyback at the top. The bad: 2026 capital spending drifted from $385–415 million to roughly $500 million within five months, San Gabriel needs another $20–25 million on top of a roughly $750 million build, and the board doubled the dividend payout ratio from 20% to 40% in February 2026 with gold near $4,500 and silver near $100, tying it explicitly to prices going well. Raising distributions at the cycle top is exactly the behaviour that has destroyed capital in this industry for fifty years, even when it is dressed as a policy rather than a promise.

On the regime, both chains read neutral, and there is no MINING_REGIME.md in this repository to override that. Neutral is the right call and it is the reason for the verdict. Silver has already fallen from a $94.53 first-half realisation to $60.18, and gold from $4,599 to $4,157.60. The company has not yet reported a quarter on those prices.

The torque cuts both ways and it is larger than the screener says. The proxy's 9.5% profit swing per 10% price move is too small for a producer at a 57% margin with two-thirds of revenue commodity-linked; the true figure is 12–18%. The bear case prices that honestly: silver at $45, gold at $3,600 and copper at $5.50 a pound takes direct-operations profit from roughly $1.0 billion to $0.62 billion and the parts to about $23.50 a share, 27% below the quote. A full bust — $38 silver, $3,200 gold — takes it to about $15, below the $17.34 low of the past twelve months. That is what an unhedged book with 1.2 times gold beta means.

Against that, the value case is genuinely there. Freeport-McMoRan's own second-quarter 2026 open-market purchase of Cerro Verde stock at $53.50 a share values Buenaventura's 19.58% holding at $3.67 billion — 45% of the entire market capitalisation — and it is invisible on the balance sheet. Credit it conservatively at $3.12 billion, add $0.18 billion of net cash and the July dividend, and the market is paying about $4.9 billion for a business earning roughly $1.0 billion at today's metals: about 5 times, against silver peers at 8 to 12. That gap is why the value score sits at four while the execution score sits at three. What holds the value score back from a five is precisely that the trailing multiple flatters — the earnings base is a peak-price photograph, and repriced at spot the consolidated multiple is ordinary rather than cheap.

So: the parts are worth about $37 a share against $32 today. Sixteen percent of upside against twenty-seven percent of adverse-case downside is not a trade you take with real money, particularly with a growth project that has been guided down three times in nine months and a metal price still falling. The specific level to wait for is **$27**, where the Cerro Verde stake plus net cash plus the direct business at a trough 4.5 times multiple already covers the whole share price and San Gabriel, Trapiche and Coimolache come free. The specific development that would substitute for that price is the October 2026 third-quarter result confirming three things at once: San Gabriel's tailings compaction actually started, the 25,000–30,000 ounce guidance survived, and Yumpag's cost fell the promised 15–17%. Either the price or that confirmation would move this to a buy. Neither is here yet.
peer_comps_note:
Buenaventura sits inside two chains — precious metals and copper mining — and needs to be checked against both, because the peer set the screener assigns (Pan American Silver, Hecla Mining, Freeport-McMoRan, Southern Copper, First Majestic, Coeur Mining, Hochschild) spans the whole range.

On enterprise value to trailing profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, all as of 2026-08-04: Buenaventura 5.31 times, Pan American Silver 8.25 times, Hecla Mining 12.02 times, Freeport-McMoRan 11.49 times. On margin, which is the better cost-curve proxy: Buenaventura 68.8% on the screener's consolidated definition and 57.5% on the company's own first-half direct-operations basis, Pan American Silver 55.7%, Hecla Mining 53.7%, Freeport-McMoRan 34.8%. On returns: Buenaventura's return on equity of 27.6% and return on invested capital of 13.3% beat Pan American Silver (19.7% and 12.5%), Hecla Mining (11.0% and 15.4%) and Freeport-McMoRan (15.3% and 8.8%).

So Buenaventura is the cheapest, highest-return and highest-margin name in its own peer set on trailing figures — which is exactly the pattern that should make a careful buyer suspicious rather than eager. Two things explain most of it. The first is legitimate and creates the opportunity: about 45% of the market capitalisation is a non-consolidated 19.58% stake in Cerro Verde whose earnings show up below the operating line, so any headline multiple on Buenaventura is comparing a partly-holding-company structure to pure operators. The second is not: the trailing profit was earned at $94.53 silver against $60.18 today, and Buenaventura's realised prices fell harder than its peers' because silver is roughly half its metal value.

The multiple I actually use for the sum-of-the-parts — 5.5 times on the spot-repriced direct business — is therefore a two-thirds discount to Pan American Silver, and I think that discount is earned rather than a mispricing: single-country Peru exposure with an unresolved election, no consolidated all-in sustaining cost disclosure, no hedging, late-life legacy mines under a stalled sale process, and a growth project guided down three times in nine months. Pan American Silver has none of those. The residual gap after all of that is what the value case rests on, and it is real but modest.
